frameworks.name: LTV to CAC Ratio (LTGP:CAC)
frameworks.definition: A ratio between lifetime gross profit (total revenue from a customer minus cost of delivery) and customer acquisition cost (all marketing and sales spend divided by customers acquired); the single number that predicts how far a business can scale advertising and how profitable it can become.

frameworks.name: LTV Stack Architecture (back-to-front)
frameworks.definition: Building lifetime gross profit by designing from the most expensive back-end offer first, then working forward so each front-end customer can be ascended through cross-sells and upsells, increasing average LTV without changing CAC.

frameworks.name: CAC Funnel Optimization (front-to-back)
frameworks.definition: Improving cost-to-acquire by working from the earliest funnel stage (ad creative and offer) toward later stages (show rate, close rate), because early-stage improvements affect the largest percentage of prospects and yield the highest order-of-magnitude impact.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi defines lifetime value (LTV) in business as lifetime gross profit: the total revenue collected from a customer minus the cost of delivering the service or product, not simply total payments received. Using total payments without subtracting cost of delivery produces a figure that cannot be reinvested or taken as profit, and treating it as LTV causes businesses to overestimate their economic engine.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Only gross profit — not revenue — can be reinvested in growth or taken out by the owner; conflating the two masks how little the business actually earns per customer.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi calculates customer acquisition cost (CAC) as total monthly marketing payroll plus total media ad spend plus total sales commissions, divided by the number of new customers acquired in the same period. Measuring CAC over a full year rather than a single month removes volatility from campaign swings and gives a number that reflects the true average cost.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a business with a 100:1 LTGP-to-CAC ratio can become ten times less efficient at advertising and still generate a 10:1 return, which means a high ratio is an ethical competitive moat: the business can outbid every competitor in ad auctions and take their customers without illegal behavior.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: business has a reliable, repeatable channel for acquiring customers
claims.mechanism: Advertising marketplaces are auctions; the highest bidder wins the eyeball. If one business can outspend 100% of competitors at any bid price and still remain profitable, it captures all available demand from that channel.

numbers.axis: LTGP:CAC ratio and advertising efficiency slack

anchors.value: thin margin; a 2x increase in CAC eliminates profitability
business can be 10x less efficient and still return 10:1 on spend

bounded_by: Does not apply when total addressable market (TAM) is too small to absorb additional spend

claims.text: Alex Hormozi observes that monthly churn rate can be used to calculate a hypothetical average customer lifetime even before long-term data exists: divide the monthly price by the monthly churn percentage to get the equivalent lifetime value (e.g., $2,000 price at 20% monthly churn = $10,000 LTV; equivalently, 1 / 20% = 5 months average retention times $2,000 = $10,000).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: churn rate is stable and measurable on a monthly cohort basis
claims.mechanism: Churn rate is the inverse of average retention duration; dividing by churn yields expected lifetime; multiplying by gross profit per period yields LTGP.

numbers.axis: LTV calculation from price and churn rate

anchors.region: 10% monthly churn at any price P

bounded_by: Does not apply to transactional non-recurring businesses where churn is not the relevant metric

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that most businesses plateau below $3 million in annual revenue specifically because they do not track LTGP-to-CAC and therefore cannot systematically invest in growth. Only approximately 1 in 250 businesses reaches $10 million per year in revenue, and his view is that knowing this ratio and maximizing it is the core practice that separates the rare 1-in-250 from the rest.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Without LTGP:CAC, a business cannot predict how much it can spend on acquisition or what return it will get, making consistent scaling impossible; it operates on hope rather than math.

anchors.region: businesses that do not track LTGP:CAC

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that when a business's LTGP:CAC ratio is very high, the correct strategy is to push as much volume as possible through that acquisition machine as fast as possible, because such ratios are temporary — market conditions, competition, and audience saturation erode them over time.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: jam as much as you possibly can through that machine
conditions: LTGP:CAC ratio is genuinely high (e.g., above 30:1)
TAM is large enough to absorb increased spend without rapid saturation
claims.mechanism: Advertising channels are competitive auctions; a high ratio creates a temporary edge that competitors will narrow as they see your growth and match or improve offers. Maximizing volume during the window captures the most lifetime customers before the edge closes.
bounded_by: Does not apply when TAM is small and saturating quickly

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that as a business scales, CAC rises because it must reach colder, harder-to-reach audiences and open new channels, so the only sustainable path to continued growth is expanding LTV — making each customer worth more — rather than just finding cheaper acquisition methods.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: business has already exhausted its warm/core audience in primary channels
claims.mechanism: Warm audiences convert at lower CAC; as they are exhausted, marketers must enter colder audiences where trust is lower and conversion is harder, raising CAC. LTV expansion is not subject to audience exhaustion: the same customer pool can be worth more through better offers, cross-sells, and price increases.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that among businesses in the same industry category, the CAC to reach a given customer type tends to be similar across competitors; what separates dominant businesses from also-rans is the LTV they have stacked on top of the same CAC, not a structural CAC advantage.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: businesses are targeting the same customer avatar in the same channel
claims.mechanism: The cost to put an ad in front of a specific person is set by the auction; all bidders pay roughly the same price for the same eyeball. What differentiates winners is how much they earn from that eyeball after acquisition.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi identifies eight ways to increase LTV (lifetime gross profit per customer): (1) increase price, (2) decrease cost of delivery, (3) get customers to buy more times (frequency), (4) cross-sell a different product, (5) upsell a better version, (6) sell a higher quantity per purchase, (7) downsell a smaller/cheaper version to convert would-be non-buyers, and (8) combinations of the above. Every product on the market has a version of each of these levers.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Alex Hormozi's framework for improving LTGP is to design the offer stack back-to-front: identify the highest-margin, highest-price back-end offer first, then build the front-end to funnel customers toward it. The front-end should have the strongest LTGP:CAC ratio; the back-end stacks additional gross profit on top of each acquired customer at near-zero incremental CAC.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: multiple offers exist at different price points targeting a related problem progression
claims.mechanism: Customers acquired through the front-end already trust the brand; selling the back-end to them costs essentially nothing in additional CAC, making every back-end conversion pure margin added to the LTV of the front-end cohort.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi's framework for reducing CAC is to optimize the funnel front-to-back: improve ad creative and offer first because they touch 100% of prospects, then work down to show rate and close rate which affect smaller sub-populations. He treats show-rate and close-rate as near-impossible to multiply by an order of magnitude (e.g., show rate cannot go from 60% to 180%), whereas click-through rate can go from 1% to 3% with better creative.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Funnel improvements are bounded at 100%; stages that are already operating near their upper bound yield small gains. Early stages (ad creative, offer, headline) operate far below their ceiling and affect the largest volume of people, so improvement there produces the highest order-of-magnitude impact on CAC.

numbers.axis: Order-of-magnitude gain possible per funnel stage

anchors.value: bounded near 60% industry avg; cannot exceed 100%

bounded_by: Exception: when a mid-funnel metric is a clear outlier (e.g., 5% show rate vs 60% industry average), fix that constraint first regardless of position in funnel

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that when a business has multiple front-end offers, the correct decision about which to advertise is determined by LTGP:CAC ratio, not by revenue size, owner preference, or customer enjoyment. The offer with the highest ratio should be advertised first; all other offers should be positioned as back-end ascension paths from the winning front-end.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: TAM for the winning offer is not saturated
claims.mechanism: LTGP:CAC determines how aggressively you can advertise; the higher-ratio offer gives more margin to outbid competitors and reach colder audiences, enabling faster customer accumulation. Stacking back-end offers behind it gives additional LTV at zero extra CAC.
bounded_by: Exception: if TAM for the best-ratio offer is too small to justify focusing on it exclusively

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a more productized, lower-ticket, faster-to-deliver service can have a higher LTGP:CAC ratio than a larger-ticket custom service, because the cost of goods sold is lower, the delivery cycle is shorter, and the TAM is typically larger. The right business to scale is the one with the highest ratio and largest TAM, not the highest ticket.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: A lower ticket with low COGS and fast delivery allows more acquisition cycles per unit time, which compounds LTV and reduces per-unit fixed cost allocation; a high-ticket custom service has high COGS, long delivery cycles, and a narrow TAM that saturates quickly.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that at scale, the daily-to-annual activities of a founder in any vertical — books, pools, shower doors, marketing agencies — converge to the same operational structure: a head of sales, head of marketing, legal, IT, finance, and operations all reporting to the founder. Therefore, the industry of the business matters less than selecting the one with the highest probability of success (best LTGP:CAC and TAM), because the founder's day-to-day ends up identical regardless.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: business at the highest level is all the same
conditions: business is scaled to the point where the founder manages a full executive team
bounded_by: Applies only to the late-stage org structure, not to early-stage execution which varies by industry

claims.text: Alex Hormozi reports that during the first year of Gym Launch, his LTGP:CAC ratio was 100:1: he spent $100,000 on customer acquisition and generated $10,000,000 in lifetime gross profit. He identifies this period as the primary source of his net worth reaching $100 million by age 31, and frames it as a punctuated event rather than gradual accumulation.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Gym Launch, year one of operations
bounded_by: This was an extreme outlier; Hormozi frames 100:1 ratios as rare and temporary

examples.text: A Facebook ads agency told Alex Hormozi they were getting a 5:1 return — spending $2,000 to acquire a customer worth $10,000 — but were losing money every month. Hormozi broke down the LTGP: the customer paid $2,000/month and stayed 5 months on average (20% monthly churn), giving $10,000 gross revenue. But the agency spent $1,000/month per account on ad spend and paid each account rep $5,000/month to manage five accounts ($1,000 per account in rep cost). Total cost per account per month: $1,000 (ads) + $1,000 (rep allocation) = $2,000. Revenue per account per month: $2,000. Net gross profit: $0. The agency had built a machine that converted $2,000 into $0, while believing they had a 5:1 return because they excluded delivery costs from LTV.

Starbucks has a lifetime customer value of $14,099 — accumulated through $5-$6 beverages over years and years of repeat visits. Alex Hormozi estimated that a local food business acquiring a similar customer through a free-cookie-with-beverage ad campaign costs approximately $10 per customer (under $1 lead cost, 1-in-10 leads walk in). At $14,099 LTV and $10 CAC, the ratio is approximately 1,400:1. Hormozi used this as an illustration of how a high LTV:CAC ratio enabled Starbucks to fund 38,000 corporate-owned stores without heavy franchising, because the economic machine was so efficient that capital cost of new locations could be recovered quickly.

A hairstylist business owner told Alex Hormozi she was running ads for two separate front-end offers simultaneously: a $2,000 digital course teaching other stylists how to install hair extensions (LTGP:CAC = 34:1, costing ~$67 to acquire), and a $15,000 business coaching program (LTGP:CAC = ~7:1, costing ~$2,000 to acquire). Hormozi identified that the extension course had a larger TAM and a dramatically better ratio. His advice: stop advertising the coaching program, make it the back-end to the extension course, and ascend buyers. If 20% of extension-course buyers (1 in 5) also bought the $15,000 coaching program, average LTGP would rise from $2,000 to $5,000 ($2,000 + 20% x $15,000 = $5,000), lifting the LTGP:CAC ratio from 30:1 to 75:1 with no increase in CAC.

A glass repair business had a full product stack including custom glass work for high-end million-dollar homes. One partner broke off to focus exclusively on shower door replacement. Shower doors were easy to sell (large TAM, broad demand), cheap to deliver (one installer could do 5-10 doors per day vs. custom glass taking months), and had low COGS. Even though the ticket was smaller than custom glass work, the LTGP:CAC ratio was higher and the delivery could be productized and repeated at high volume. Hormozi used this to illustrate that average ticket size does not predict LTGP:CAC; the combination of COGS, delivery speed, and TAM determines the ratio.

A pool designer told Alex Hormozi he designed commercial pools, resort pools, residential pools, and modular pools. Modular pools had only six or seven variables, could be assembled quickly (short cycle from signed contract to installation), had good margins, and had a much larger TAM than resort pools. The other types were all custom one-off projects, difficult to systematize, and served narrow segments. Hormozi advised him to focus on modular pools: highest LTGP:CAC, largest TAM, fastest delivery loop, and highest productization potential — all four of which compound to create a scalable, repeatable machine.

A business coach doing $3 million per year did not know his LTGP:CAC ratio. When Alex Hormozi asked him, he said he didn't know. Hormozi repeatedly responded: 'know your data so that you can scale your company.' The coach kept asking other questions; Hormozi kept returning to the same point. Hormozi used this story to illustrate that operating without LTGP:CAC data is why businesses stay stuck below $10 million in revenue, regardless of what advice they seek or what tactics they try.

practices.text: Calculate CAC on an annual basis — total marketing payroll + total ad spend + total sales commissions for the full year, divided by total new customers acquired in the year — to eliminate volatility from individual campaign swings, good or bad sales days, and outlier months.

For service businesses with employees dedicated to delivery, calculate cost of goods sold per customer by dividing total delivery payroll by number of active customers; update this calculation as customer count changes to model per-unit delivery cost at scale.

When you have multiple front-end offers, identify which has the highest LTGP:CAC ratio, allocate your advertising budget to that offer first, and position all other offers as back-end ascension paths for customers acquired through the winning front-end.
If your business has a high LTGP:CAC ratio and large TAM, push as much volume through that acquisition machine as fast as possible before competitors and market saturation erode the edge.

Evaluate every product through eight LTV levers: raise price, lower COGS, increase purchase frequency, cross-sell a different product, upsell a better version, bundle a higher quantity, downsell a cheaper version, or reduce unit quantity for a lower-price option.

When optimizing CAC, work front-to-back through the funnel: start with ad creative and offer (highest leverage, affects 100% of prospects), then headline and landing page, then availability and show rate, then close rate — unless a mid-funnel metric is a clear outlier compared to industry benchmarks.
